title: A Boston University Grad Posted a Google Form. 100,000 Indians Joined His Satirical Political Party in Three Days.
excerpt: After the Chief Justice called young Indians ‘cockroaches,’ 30-year-old Abhijeet Dipke turned the slur into a movement — from his apartment in Massachusetts
body:
A 30-year-old Indian American sitting in his Boston apartment has, in the span of 72 hours, built what no established political party in India has managed in years: a platform that over 100,000 frustrated young Indians actually want to join.

## The Spark That Lit the Fuse

On May 15, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant set off a firestorm during a Supreme Court hearing on fake professional qualifications. In an oral observation, he compared certain unemployed individuals — those using fraudulent degrees to enter journalism, social media, and RTI activism — to cockroaches. He later clarified that his remark targeted credential fraud, not India’s unemployed youth broadly. But by then, the damage was done.

The comment landed in a country where youth unemployment remains a raw nerve. Exam paper leaks, stalled government recruitment drives, and a widening gulf between degree holders and available jobs have made young Indians deeply sceptical of the institutions meant to serve them. The CJI’s words, intended or not, crystallised that anger.

## Enter Abhijeet Dipke

Within 24 hours, Abhijeet Dipke — a freshly minted Master’s in Public Relations from Boston University — posted a Google Form on X with a pitch dripping in self-aware irony. “Launching a new platform for all the cockroaches out there,” he wrote. “Eligibility criteria: Unemployed. Lazy. Chronically online. Ability to rant professionally.”

By morning, 15,000 people had signed up.

Dipke is no stranger to Indian political internet culture. Before moving to the US, the Aurangabad native studied journalism in Pune and ran the social media blitz behind AAP’s 2020 Delhi assembly campaign — the meme avalanche widely credited with boosting Arvind Kejriwal’s commanding win. He spent 2020 to 2022 as a social media coordinator for the party before pursuing his American degree.

“The Cockroach Janta Party was supposed to be a joke,” Dipke told LiveMint from Boston. “But I had not expected it would draw such an encouraging response. Seems the youth of our country identify with it.”

## A Joke That Outgrew the Punchline

The numbers tell the story. As of May 19, the movement has crossed 100,000 sign-ups through its official portal cockroachjantaparty.org. Its Instagram page counts 12,000 followers; its X account, nearly 29,000. The party’s satirical tagline — “Secular, Socialist, Democratic and Lazy” — has become a meme in its own right.

But what started as internet comedy has developed surprisingly structured ambitions. The CJP’s five-point manifesto demands a complete ban on post-retirement Rajya Sabha seats for Chief Justices, 50 percent women’s reservation in cabinet posts, a 20-year electoral ban for party-switching politicians, and full RTI accountability with no anonymous donations. Its official election symbol? A smartphone.

The movement has drawn real political attention. Trinamool Congress MPs Mahua Moitra and Kirti Azad both publicly engaged with the platform. “I too would like to join the CJP,” Moitra posted on X. Prominent lawyers, academics, and RTI activists like Anjali Bhardwaj have also weighed in with policy suggestions.

Perhaps most striking: groups of young volunteers wearing “I am a cockroach” placards have begun conducting public cleanup drives near garbage dumps and water bodies — turning the insult into visible civic action.

## The NRI Who Might Come Home

For the Indian diaspora, Dipke’s story inverts the familiar brain-drain narrative. Here is an NRI who leveraged an American education in media strategy to channel a domestic Indian frustration into a movement that resonated instantly — and who is now considering moving back.

“I have a lot of pressure. I get hundreds of messages,” Dipke said. “I cannot disappoint those who have responded. I think I will be in India soon, and we will think what to do with the movement. We have 100,000 sign-ups. It can’t be left as such.”

Whether the Cockroach Janta Party evolves into something more durable — or remains a brilliant, pointed flash of internet-age protest — may depend on what Dipke does next. India’s youth, it turns out, were waiting for someone to say what they already felt. They just did not expect the invitation to come from a Google Form posted from Massachusetts.
